newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia gold output may fall further on price dip.
newsitem.headline: Russia gold output may fall further on price dip.

text.p: Tarnished world gold prices could further depress Russia's declining gold output, industry officials said on Tuesday.
"Of course it will affect things," said Vladimir Rybkin, head of the Finance Ministry's precious metals section. "But I cannot tell you by how much."
He said Russian gold output would not slip below 100 tonnes this year but declined to give a specific forecast.
Various mining officials have forecast Russia's 1997 gold output in a range of 95-110 tonnes, down from about 124 tonnes in 1996. Some officials have said last year's output was as low as 101 tonnes.
Central Bank Deputy Chairman Alexander Potyomkin told a briefing on Tuesday Russia would have to work to cut costs.

"Look where the problem is -- the world market price for gold is falling quickly," he said. "In dollar equivalent terms, the price has already killed mining costs in far-flung regions. The only means now to revive work and mining is in cutting costs."
The world price of gold has slumped to 11-1/2 year lows of around $317 an ounce on news of selling by Australia's central bank.
Russian gold output has fallen because the state does not have enough cash to finance output and because there are almost no ways for banks to finance any significant production volumes.
Sergei Kyshtymov, head of the Russian central bank's precious metals department, said Russian output was too expensive to be competitive.
Russia keeps a tight lid on its gold industry. Moscow says it is working to liberalise the sector so banks can finance output but little progress has been made.
Russian central bank reserves were 397 tonnes as of April 20, the last date for which data was available. The bank has said it aims to increase reserves by 90 tonnes a year over 1997 and 1998.
